Any and all of them would be panned by some people, just because the internet tends to bring out the shallowness and bitterness of people, and some of them manifest that by condemning anything and everything that might ever appear on one or another site.

Some of them would be panned by many, since the works became famous not so much for their merits as because of their position in history. I would think that would especially be the case for minimalist and/or post-modernist abstracts (Mondrian, Klee, Pollock, Warhol...), many of which gained favor in the first place because they came at times when the dominant trends in high-end gallery art had become bloated and stagnant, and they provided refreshing clarity and simplicity. An art world that was beginning to grow tired of seeing yet another dusk-lit Athenian temple crammed full of painstakingly detailed greenery and nymphets in diaphanous gowns suddenly came across a single slash of color perfectly placed on a monochrome field and were moved by the rebellious simplicity of it. Now, on dA, most people wouldn't even click on the thumbnail.

I wonder about the middle ground - the works that appeal more to the artistically-inclined and less to the rest of the world (Van Gogh, Picasso, Dali...) and the works that appeal more to the rest of the world and less to the artistically-inclined (Escher, Frazetta, Kincade...) I would tend to think, just by the nature of the internet, that the former would be less famous and the latter more.

The thing with dA too though, and with the internet in general, is that an awful lot of things that really deserve recognition would certainly slip through the cracks, just because there's so much media out there competing for clicks. And even the things that gain considerable recognition soon wane, replaced by the next thing that earns a click.
